one_liner: Tiny 128-bit-state add-rotate PRNG; author's gcc benchmark: 0.401 ns/call vs xoroshiro128++ 0.829, tied with wyrand.
what_it_does: A non-cryptographic generator with two 64-bit state words and 64-bit output, meant to be seeded with SplitMix64. There is no library or API: the algorithm is the five-line dualMix128() function in the README, and the repo holds only benchmark.c, its output, PractRand and BigCrush driver programs, and an MIT license, so you paste the function into your code. The README marks it superseded by the author's LoopMix128, which it says has proven injectivity and a guaranteed 2^128 period.
how_it_is_fast: Each step is one add (mix = s0 + s1), two rotates and two adds for the new state, and one multiply of mix by the golden-ratio constant for the output. The loop-carried dependency is only about two adds deep and the multiply sits off the critical path, while xoroshiro128++'s update chains xor, rotate, shift and xor. The state update is a nonlinear add-rotate mix with a multiplicative output scrambler, so no linear-algebra structure and no jump function.
when_to_use: Hot scalar loops (Monte Carlo, procedural generation, randomized testing) where a single 64-bit draw per call must be as cheap as possible and PractRand/BigCrush-level quality is enough.
When a 16-byte, multiply-free state update is wanted, e.g. one generator embedded per object or per thread.
As a reference for the design line that continued in LoopMix128 and biski64.
when_not_to_use: When you need a guaranteed period: injectivity is unproven (the README strikes its 'possibly injective' claim), so the period and the risk of short cycles are unknown; the author points to LoopMix128 instead.
Parallel simulations that need non-overlapping streams: there is no jump or stream function.
Anything security-sensitive: the README says it is for non-cryptographic use.
When wyrand is already available: the author's own benchmark has wyrand at the same 0.401 ns/call.
When you want a maintained, packaged library: 23 commits, 4 stars, no header or API, and the LoopMix128 link now redirects to the biski64 repository.

integration.form: source-drop (copy the function from the README or benchmark.c)
integration.min_toolchain: C99 (stdint.h); the published benchmark was built with gcc 11.4.0 -O3 -march=native
integration.platforms: any platform with 64-bit integers (portable C, no intrinsics; the benchmark harness uses POSIX clock_gettime)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the reference code keeps state in global variables, so move it into a per-thread struct
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same 128-bit state and 64-bit output as xoroshiro128++, but a different sequence and no jump()/long_jump()

gotchas: The all-zero state is a fixed point (mix = 0 keeps both words 0 and the output stays 0 forever); benchmark.c's seed function does not check for it, so seed through SplitMix64 as test_practrand.c does.
The reference code uses global state and non-static 'inline' functions, which under C99 inline rules can fail to link at -O0; wrap it as a static inline function over a state struct.

The timing is single-stream latency with a volatile store per call, and the CPU is not stated; DualMix128 and wyrand land on the identical 0.401 ns, which suggests a loop or store floor rather than a measured difference between them.
The README's Java claims (27% faster than Java xoroshiro128++, 8.82x java.util.Random) have no Java code or output in the repo.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Rarely: wyrand ties it in its own benchmark with 8 bytes of state and a Weyl-sequence period of 2^64, biski64 (already catalogued; the LoopMix128 link now lands there) is the author's later design with a guaranteed minimum period, and Sirius64, Romu or the xoshiro family are better analysed. Choose DualMix128 only if you specifically want its multiply-free 16-byte state update and accept an unknown period.
verified_claims_summary: benchmark.out (gcc 11.4.0 on Ubuntu 22.04, -O3 -march=native, CPU not stated) times 10^10 single-stream calls each storing to a volatile: DualMix128 0.401 ns/call, xoroshiro128++ 0.829 ns (about 2.07x, derived from page data), wyrand 0.401 ns. The xoroshiro128++ in benchmark.c is the standard algorithm, so the gap mostly reflects xoroshiro's longer dependency chain.
status_note: Stale (last commit 2025-05-10) and superseded by its author, but MIT-licensed and five lines long, so copying is trivial; prefer the successor if you need a period guarantee.
